quarterly_data.quarter: Honeywell Aerospace Jefferies Global Industrials Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Currier: Honeywell Aerospace had over $17.5 billion in sales last year, has secured over $105 billion worth of lifetime contract wins over the last couple of years, and its backlog is over $18 billion, up over 9% year on year, with book-to-bill over 1.1 across the portfolio; 90% of all aircraft flying in the free world have Honeywell content. 'We're not seeing any erosion to our demand' - the issue is executing out of the supply base, which defers revenue.
quarterly_data.figure: backlog over $18 billion (up over 9%); book-to-bill over 1.1; over $105 billion lifetime contract wins; sales last year over $17.5 billion

quarterly_data.quarter: Honeywell Aerospace Jefferies Global Industrials Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Currier, supplier scorecard: over 3,000 suppliers are meeting plan; about 70 are critical or constrained, of which about 10 are constrained - in complex machining, castings, forgings and bearings, with bearings the most constrained; the electronics portion (40% of the portfolio) has recovered. Proof points: 35% of the yearly output needed for high-volume bearings was delivered in the last three months, mainly the last six weeks, as a second source kicks in and past dues burn down; in castings and forgings (concentrated among a top four or five providers) Honeywell Aerospace is locking up additional capacity, giving long-term demand profiles and bringing tooling online; at two critical complex-machining suppliers constrained by skilled labor it inserted dozens of its own skilled workers over the last 30 to 45 days, for about a 20% year-on-year output improvement over the last 30 days. Some bearing suppliers are setting up dedicated production lines for Honeywell Aerospace products. It has long-term contracts with Consolidated Precision Products (CPP) and invests in CPP's tooling, yield and quality; its CPP business does not overlap GE's, and he expects GE acquiring CPP to benefit the industry and Honeywell Aerospace. He is 'very confident' in improved output growth in 2027 and beyond.
quarterly_data.figure: about 70 critical / constrained suppliers, about 10 constrained (of over 3,000); 35% of yearly high-volume bearing output in the last three months; about 20% output improvement at complex machining

quarterly_data.quarter: Honeywell Aerospace Jefferies Global Industrials Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Currier on investment: over $1 billion has gone into the supply base since August 2023 (about 70% external, 30% internal), including a dedicated circuit card assembly line at the Olathe facility for $100 million to insource electronics work; going forward an equal dollar amount will be invested over the next couple of years on an accelerated timeline, moving investments into 2026 and from 2028 into 2027 - for example accelerating $50 million of capex from 2027 into 2026. Honeywell Aerospace funds supplier tooling and, where suppliers are unwilling or cannot afford it, capital expansion projects, and embeds skilled labor. RD&E is north of 4% of revenue, over 10% including customer funding. He expects the supply base being built to be able to double the size of the business within the next 10 years.
quarterly_data.figure: $100 million Olathe circuit card assembly line; $50 million capex moved from 2027 into 2026; RD&E north of 4% of revenue (over 10% with customer funding)

quarterly_data.quarter: Honeywell Aerospace Jefferies Global Industrials Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Currier on the commercial business: the commercial aftermarket is 40% of the business, 60% commercial air transport and 40% business aviation, with demand strongest in super mid-size to ultra-long-range business jets; retrofit mods and upgrades are about 10% of the business, growing double digit; many business-aviation contracts are power-by-the-hour, and he expects commercial aftermarket growth in excess of flight hours. In selectables Honeywell Aerospace historically won around 40% of the value competed and now 60% over the last 4,000 aircraft wins; IndiGo (800 aircraft) is the largest win, second a United Airlines win of 600 aircraft a couple of years ago. Margin expansion will come mostly from volume, then mix (more output to the aftermarket) and price as long-term agreements with multiple OEMs are renegotiated.
quarterly_data.figure: aftermarket 40% of business (60% air transport / 40% business aviation); retrofit, mods and upgrades about 10%; selectables win rate around 40% historically, 60% over the last 4,000 aircraft; United Airlines 600 aircraft
